tools.name: React
tools.purpose: Build interfaces out of reusable components that update as data changes.
tools.example: A message list that updates when a new reply arrives.
tools.distinction: Next.js builds on React. They are different layers, rather than equivalent alternatives.

tools.name: Next.js
tools.purpose: Build a web application with pages, routing, server rendering and server-side code.
tools.example: A paid app with a public homepage, dashboard and server endpoints.
tools.distinction: Uses React for interfaces. It does not require Vercel; other deployment setups are possible.

tools.name: shadcn/ui
tools.purpose: Start with useful interface component code that you can own and adapt.
tools.example: Add a dialog, dropdown or form without designing every interaction from scratch.
tools.distinction: Provides components; Tailwind handles styling. They commonly work together.

tools.name: Tailwind CSS
tools.purpose: Style layouts and interface elements with utility classes.
tools.example: Set a dashboard’s spacing, responsive columns and colors.
tools.distinction: Styles the interface; it does not implement application behavior.

tools.name: Framer Motion
tools.purpose: Animate React interfaces with transitions, gestures and coordinated layout changes.
tools.example: Animate a card expanding, a dialog entering or items rearranging in a list.
tools.distinction: Now called Motion for React. It adds animation to React interfaces; it is separate from the Framer website builder.

tools.name: next-intl
tools.purpose: Add translated messages and locale-aware formatting to Next.js applications.
tools.example: Offer a dashboard in German and English with appropriate number and date formatting.

tools.name: React Native
tools.purpose: Use React to build interfaces backed by native platform components on iOS and Android.
tools.example: Build a mobile app with native screens, buttons and device interactions.
tools.distinction: Uses React concepts, but native components differ from browser HTML elements. Expo provides a framework around React Native.

tools.name: Expo
tools.purpose: Build React Native apps with routing, native modules and development tooling.
tools.example: Create an iOS and Android app with navigation, camera access and a shared codebase.
tools.distinction: Builds on React Native. Expo Application Services (EAS) add optional services such as cloud builds and app submission.

tools.name: Three.js
tools.purpose: Create and render interactive 3D scenes in the browser with cameras, lighting and materials.
tools.example: Let someone rotate a 3D product model on a website.
tools.distinction: Handles 3D scenes; it is not a general UI framework and does not require React. Motion focuses on interface animation.

tools.name: React Three Fiber
tools.purpose: Build Three.js scenes using React components, props and state.
tools.example: Create an interactive 3D product viewer whose colors and camera respond to React UI controls.
tools.distinction: Uses Three.js underneath rather than replacing it. React describes and updates the scene; Three.js provides the 3D graphics functionality.

tools.name: Payload CMS
tools.purpose: Give editors an admin interface for managing structured content, and make that content available to your application.
tools.example: Let someone update articles, landing-page copy and media without editing the website code.
tools.distinction: A CMS manages content and editing workflows. Your frontend controls how that content is presented; Payload is built on Next.js.

tools.name: Stripe
tools.purpose: Accept customer payments and manage billing flows.
tools.example: Sell a recurring subscription to your application.
tools.distinction: Customer payments are a separate job from provisioning services through Stripe Projects.

tools.name: Resend
tools.purpose: Send emails from application code.
tools.example: Send a welcome message or order confirmation after a user action.
tools.distinction: Application email delivery serves a different primary need from hosting your personal mailboxes.

tools.name: PostHog
tools.purpose: Understand how people use your product and where they encounter friction.
tools.example: See how many people move from signing up to completing their first task.

tools.name: Apollo.io
tools.purpose: Find business contacts and companies, enrich prospect information and organize sales outreach.
tools.example: Research companies that could benefit from a product and organize a list of potential customers.
tools.distinction: A sales tool around the business, not an application framework. Unrelated to Apollo GraphQL.

tools.name: Migadu
tools.purpose: Host email addresses and mailboxes for your domains.
tools.example: Receive and send personal correspondence at your own domain.
tools.distinction: Mailbox hosting differs from Resend’s primary application-email role.

tools.name: Neon
tools.purpose: Host the database that persists your application’s information.
tools.example: Keep users, conversations and subscription records between visits.
tools.distinction: PostgreSQL is the underlying database technology; Neon provides a managed service around it.

tools.name: Supabase
tools.purpose: Combine a Postgres database with services for sign-in, file storage, realtime updates and backend functions.
tools.example: Build a shared app with user accounts, saved records and uploaded files.
tools.distinction: Its database overlaps with Neon; its auth and storage services overlap with roles served by Better Auth and R2. These are separate capabilities, not automatic drop-in replacements.

tools.name: Drizzle
tools.purpose: Describe database schemas and query SQL databases from TypeScript.
tools.example: Read a customer’s orders from PostgreSQL hosted by Neon.
tools.distinction: Runs in your application’s data-access layer; it does not host the database.

tools.name: TanStack Query
tools.purpose: Fetch, cache and synchronize server data in the interface.
tools.example: Refresh an order list after a purchase without manually coordinating every request.
tools.distinction: Manages the UI’s view of remote data. It is not a database or an SQL query builder.

tools.name: Better Auth
tools.purpose: Add user accounts, sign-in methods and session management to an application.
tools.example: Let people sign in to a Next.js dashboard and maintain their session.
tools.distinction: Authentication establishes who a user is. Your application still needs authorization rules for what that user may access.

tools.name: Clerk
tools.purpose: Add sign-up, sign-in, sessions and user management with hosted services and ready-made UI components.
tools.example: Add a sign-in screen and account menu to a Next.js app, including organization membership for teams.
tools.distinction: Clerk operates the authentication service. Better Auth is a framework integrated into your own backend. Both solve sign-in and session needs with different operating models.

tools.name: Cloudflare R2
tools.purpose: Store and retrieve file contents such as images, PDFs, video and audio.
tools.example: Keep uploaded audio in R2 while Neon stores its owner, filename and other structured records.
tools.distinction: Object storage holds files; a relational database organizes records and relationships. R2 and Neon can complement each other.

tools.name: Effect
tools.purpose: Structure programs with explicit error handling, concurrency and resource lifetimes.
tools.example: Coordinate several service calls, handle failures and release resources reliably.
tools.distinction: Can support application logic across layers; its placement here describes its main job.

tools.name: AI SDK
tools.purpose: Connect application code to AI model providers and build interactions such as streaming responses.
tools.example: Stream an AI reply into your app’s chat interface.
tools.distinction: The SDK is integration code, not the AI model. A model/provider is an additional choice.

tools.name: Vercel AI Gateway
tools.purpose: Access models from multiple providers through a shared API with routing and usage tracking.
tools.example: Use a model through the AI SDK and configure fallback providers for model requests.
tools.distinction: AI SDK is the application library; AI Gateway is a service that routes requests to model providers.

tools.name: Exa
tools.purpose: Give applications and AI agents access to web search results and page content.
tools.example: Let a research assistant find relevant webpages and retrieve their contents as evidence.
tools.distinction: Supplies external information for a model to use. A model gateway routes model calls; these serve different parts of an AI workflow.

tools.name: ElevenLabs
tools.purpose: Add voice and audio capabilities to a product.
tools.example: Turn an AI tutor’s text response into spoken audio.

tools.name: Keyframe Labs
tools.purpose: Give an AI experience a real-time, lifelike avatar.
tools.example: Pair a conversational model and a voice service with a visual tutor.
tools.distinction: An avatar is one part of the experience; the conversational model and voice can come from other providers.

tools.name: Vercel
tools.purpose: Deploy and run web applications through a managed platform.
tools.example: Publish a Next.js application and preview changes before a release.
tools.distinction: Bundles multiple operational responsibilities. Replacing it with your own platform requires more than an orchestrator.

tools.name: Coolify
tools.purpose: Deploy and manage applications, databases and services on servers you control.
tools.example: Deploy a GitHub project to a Hetzner server with a dashboard for domains and deployments.
tools.distinction: Offers a deployment platform on your own infrastructure. It overlaps with parts of Vercel, while server maintenance remains your responsibility.

tools.name: Stripe Projects
tools.purpose: Provision supported third-party services and manage their credentials and provider billing.
tools.example: Set up a supported hosting or database service from a project workflow.
tools.distinction: Coordinates providers; it is neither a database itself nor your app’s customer payment flow.

tools.name: Hetzner
tools.purpose: Rent cloud virtual machines or dedicated servers to run applications and other workloads.
tools.example: Run a Docker-based application on a cloud server, or use several machines for a Kubernetes cluster.
tools.distinction: Provides infrastructure. You still choose and operate the deployment setup, application services and monitoring; this is a different layer from a managed app platform such as Vercel.

tools.name: Docker
tools.purpose: Build container images and run applications in isolated containers with their dependencies.
tools.example: Package a service into an image, then run it locally or publish it for deployment.
tools.distinction: Docker builds and runs containers. Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads across a cluster; it does not require Docker Engine.

tools.name: Kubernetes
tools.purpose: Schedule and manage containerized workloads across a cluster.
tools.example: Run and scale several application services on infrastructure you control.
tools.distinction: Can underpin an alternative to Vercel. Infrastructure, builds, routing and other operations still need a solution.

tools.name: Cloudflare
tools.purpose: Provide services for DNS, delivery, security and compute.
tools.example: Manage a domain’s DNS, protect traffic or run code with Workers.
tools.distinction: This name covers many products. It may complement Vercel or overlap with it depending on which services you choose.

tools.name: Tailscale
tools.purpose: Connect your devices and servers through an encrypted private network with access controls.
tools.example: Reach your Linux workstation or a private service on a Hetzner server while away from home.
tools.distinction: Connects machines; it does not host your app or replace the public deployment platform.

tools.name: Grafana
tools.purpose: See how your systems are doing through dashboards and charts.
tools.example: Watch request counts, error rates and CPU usage in one place.
tools.distinction: Grafana displays data from tools such as Prometheus; it is not the tool collecting every measurement.

tools.name: Prometheus
tools.purpose: Collect and store measurements about running systems over time.
tools.example: Track CPU usage or how many requests fail each minute.
tools.distinction: Prometheus handles measurements. Grafana can turn those measurements into dashboards.

tools.name: OpenTelemetry (OTel)
tools.purpose: Help your application report what it is doing using standard telemetry tools.
tools.example: Record how long a request takes and send that information to a monitoring system.
tools.distinction: OTel helps produce and transport telemetry; it is not a dashboard or a complete monitoring service.

tools.name: Elastic Stack (ELK)
tools.purpose: Collect, search and explore logs to understand what happened in an application.
tools.example: Find the error messages recorded when a request failed.
tools.distinction: ELK stands for Elasticsearch (search and storage), Logstash (data processing) and Kibana (exploration). Shown as one stack to keep the overview simple.

tools.name: Omarchy
tools.purpose: Provide a configured Linux desktop and development environment.
tools.example: Use a Linux workstation as the place where you write code and organize work.

tools.name: Raycast
tools.purpose: Access applications, commands and everyday workflows quickly.
tools.example: Use a keyboard-driven command to open an app or perform a frequent action.
tools.distinction: Listed as part of the broader ecosystem; this does not imply it runs on the Omarchy workstation.

tools.name: Ventoy
tools.purpose: Prepare a USB drive that can boot multiple operating-system installers and recovery images from one menu.
tools.example: Keep Linux installers and rescue tools on one USB drive, then choose which image to boot when starting a computer.
tools.distinction: Helps boot installation or recovery media. It is not an operating system itself; after setting up Ventoy, you can copy supported image files onto the drive.

tools.name: Glove80
tools.purpose: Provide the physical keyboard you use to interact with your workstation.
tools.example: Type and use shortcuts on an ergonomic split keyboard.

tools.name: Samsung ultrawide
tools.purpose: Provide a wide physical workspace for the applications you use.
tools.example: Keep code, a browser and reference material visible at once.
tools.distinction: The exact monitor model is not specified in this collection.

tools.name: Codex
tools.purpose: Help carry out software development tasks, from implementation to investigating code.
tools.example: Ask an agent to implement and verify a feature in your project.
tools.distinction: A tool used while building software, rather than a feature automatically shipped inside the product.

tools.name: Claude Code
tools.purpose: Help explore, modify and work with a software project.
tools.example: Investigate a bug or refactor a module with a coding agent.
tools.distinction: Overlaps with Codex in coding-agent work; either may fit a development task.

tools.name: Pi
tools.purpose: Use a minimal coding agent harness that can be adapted to your own development workflows.
tools.example: Customize an agent with extensions and tools to work the way your project needs.
tools.distinction: The harness connects a model to tools and a working session. Pi emphasizes a small, customizable foundation for agent workflows.

tools.name: fx
tools.purpose: Work with a coding agent through a lightweight, shell-like CLI, or embed its harness in another system.
tools.example: Ask the agent to investigate a repository interactively, or call it from a script for a focused coding task.
tools.distinction: An experimental Vercel Labs agent with support for different model providers. It is the coding harness; AI Gateway is one service it can use to access models.

tools.name: Agentation
tools.purpose: Turn annotations on a webpage into structured feedback that a coding agent can act on.
tools.example: Click a misaligned button, describe the change and give the agent the element context.
tools.distinction: You point out what should change. Agentation supplies context; the coding agent makes the code changes.

tools.name: d3k (dev3000)
tools.purpose: Give a coding agent a shared timeline of dev-server logs, browser errors, network activity and screenshots.
tools.example: Reproduce a broken checkout locally so the agent can connect the visible failure with relevant logs.
tools.distinction: A Vercel Labs development tool. It helps investigate a running local app; Grafana and Prometheus serve a different monitoring role.

tools.name: agent-browser
tools.purpose: Let an AI agent inspect and interact with websites through a browser automation CLI.
tools.example: Have an agent open a page, fill a form and check what happens after submission.
tools.distinction: Focuses on agent-driven browser interaction. Playwright also automates browsers and provides a framework for repeatable test suites.

tools.name: agent-device
tools.purpose: Let a coding agent inspect and interact with running apps on devices, simulators and emulators.
tools.example: Have an agent open an iOS or Android app, tap through a flow and inspect the resulting screen.
tools.distinction: Made by Callstack. Especially useful for mobile app verification; agent-browser focuses on the browser.

tools.name: Bun
tools.purpose: Run JavaScript and TypeScript, install packages, and provide test and build tooling.
tools.example: Install dependencies and run a project locally.
tools.distinction: Can also be used as a production runtime; tools can have roles in more than one territory.

tools.name: Bun workspaces
tools.purpose: Manage and link multiple local packages in one repository through Bun’s package manager.
tools.example: Keep a web app, mobile app and shared utilities together, with local packages depending on one another.
tools.distinction: A feature of Bun, not a separate runtime. Workspaces organize packages and dependencies; Nx or Turborepo can add task graphs and build caching.

tools.name: Nx
tools.purpose: Coordinate builds, tests and other tasks using a project graph and cached task results.
tools.example: When a shared package changes, run the checks affected by that change across your apps.
tools.distinction: Overlaps with Turborepo in task orchestration and caching. Also offers plugins and generators; package installation remains the package manager’s job.

tools.name: Turborepo
tools.purpose: Run tasks across JavaScript and TypeScript packages in dependency order and reuse cached results.
tools.example: Build shared packages before the Next.js app that uses them, skipping work whose inputs have not changed.
tools.distinction: Overlaps with Nx in builds and task caching. Works alongside package-manager workspaces; it is distinct from the Turbopack bundler.

tools.name: Husky
tools.purpose: Run project commands automatically at Git events such as committing or pushing.
tools.example: Run a lint command before a commit and stop the commit when that check fails.
tools.distinction: Runs checks you configure; it is not a linter itself. Local hooks can be bypassed, so required checks also belong in CI.

tools.name: lint-staged
tools.purpose: Run configured commands, such as formatters and linters, on matching files staged for a Git commit.
tools.example: Have Husky call lint-staged before committing, then format and lint the staged TypeScript files.
tools.distinction: Husky triggers the Git hook; lint-staged selects files and runs commands. The formatter or linter performs the actual checks. Whole-project checks still belong in CI.

tools.name: jscpd
tools.purpose: Find repeated blocks of source code and report duplication.
tools.example: Flag copied logic across files during a code-quality check or CI run.
tools.distinction: Detects textual duplication, not whether the program behaves correctly. A repeated block is a review prompt, not automatically a reason to refactor.

tools.name: Playwright
tools.purpose: Automate a real browser to check complete user interactions across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
tools.example: Test that a user can sign in, upload a file and complete an important workflow.
tools.distinction: Exercises the running application through a browser. Code-level tests cover smaller pieces of logic; the two approaches complement each other.

tools.name: GitHub
tools.purpose: Host Git repositories and collaborate through pull requests, code reviews and issues.
tools.example: Share a project, review a proposed change and merge it into the main branch.
tools.distinction: Git tracks version history; GitHub hosts repositories and adds collaboration tools. GitHub issues overlap with some work tracked in Linear.

tools.name: Linear
tools.purpose: Organize issues, projects and priorities so a team can plan and track work.
tools.example: Track a feature from idea through implementation and completion.
tools.distinction: Tracks the work to be done; GitHub hosts and reviews the code implementing it. Their issue-tracking features overlap.

tools.name: Composio
tools.purpose: Connect AI agents to external applications, with tools and authentication for using those services.
tools.example: Give an agent access to connected work apps through a common integration layer.
tools.distinction: Overlaps with Executor in connecting agents to external tools; the products have different integration and execution approaches.

tools.name: AgentMail
tools.purpose: Give AI agents dedicated email inboxes they can create and operate through an API.
tools.example: Give a support agent its own address to receive messages, read attachments and reply in the same conversation.
tools.distinction: Provides email inbox infrastructure for agents. Composio connects agents to many external apps; AgentMail focuses specifically on email.

tools.name: Executor
tools.purpose: Expose connected MCP servers, OpenAPI services and GraphQL APIs to agents through a shared gateway.
tools.example: Connect work tools once and make them available to coding agents through one MCP endpoint.
tools.distinction: A gateway to tools, rather than the coding agent itself. Listed here as an exploration, not a core dependency.

tools.name: DataForSEO
tools.purpose: Retrieve search and SEO data programmatically to build research and analysis tools.
tools.example: Build a small tool that compares search results and keyword data.
tools.distinction: Provides data APIs; you build the interface and analysis around them.

tools.name: Beeper
tools.purpose: Bring conversations from supported messaging services into one application.
tools.example: Read and reply to chats from several networks without switching between their apps.
tools.distinction: A personal messaging client. It connects to existing chat networks rather than providing messaging infrastructure for your own product.

tools.name: Notion Calendar
tools.purpose: View connected calendars and organize meetings, events and time alongside Notion.
tools.example: See your schedule in one place and block out time for focused work.
tools.distinction: A calendar application for managing your day; Linear tracks project work and issues.

tools.name: 1Password
tools.purpose: Store and organize passwords, passkeys and other sensitive credentials in vaults.
tools.example: Generate a unique password for a new service and fill it when signing in.
tools.distinction: Manages the credentials you use. Clerk and Better Auth implement sign-in for users of the apps you build.

tools.name: Ghostty
tools.purpose: Provide a terminal interface for shells and command-line programs.
tools.example: Run Bun, Git or a coding agent in a terminal window.
tools.distinction: The terminal displays and interacts with programs. Your shell interprets commands, and tools such as Bun or Pi do their own work inside it.

tools.name: Fireship
tools.purpose: Short programming explainers, developer news and technology commentary.

tools.name: Theo — t3.gg
tools.purpose: Commentary on web development, TypeScript, frameworks and developer tools.

tools.name: Y Combinator
tools.purpose: Talks, interviews and advice about building startups, making products and working with customers.

tools.name: Nate B Jones
tools.purpose: Analysis and discussion of AI developments and their practical implications.

tools.name: Two Minute Papers
tools.purpose: Accessible explanations of research in AI, computer graphics and related fields.

tools.name: Alex Hormozi
tools.purpose: Business education and commentary on offers, sales and growing a company.

tools.name: TLDR
tools.purpose: Read concise technology news summaries and follow links to the original stories.

tools.name: Luma
tools.purpose: Discover events and follow calendars to keep up with communities and upcoming gatherings.
tools.example: Follow a community calendar and get updates about upcoming meetups.
tools.distinction: An events platform, grouped here with newsletters as a source of updates and discovery.

tools.name: ThePrimeagen
tools.purpose: Programming discussions, development workflows and software engineering commentary.

tools.name: Framework Laptop
tools.purpose: Provide a portable computer for development and everyday work.
tools.example: Write code, run local projects and take your development setup with you.
tools.distinction: The physical laptop, separate from the operating system and tools installed on it. The exact model is not specified here.

tools.name: MX Master 3S
tools.purpose: Navigate, select and scroll through applications with a wireless mouse.
tools.example: Move between code, browser tabs and documents, using the main scroll wheel and thumb wheel.

tools.name: Matt Pocock’s Skills
tools.purpose: Give coding agents reusable workflows for planning, investigating and changing software.
tools.example: Use a skill to question a feature idea or break a refactor into small steps.
tools.distinction: A collection of instructions used by an agent, rather than a separate coding agent or model.

tools.name: Marketing Skills
tools.purpose: Give agents workflows for copywriting, SEO, conversion optimization and marketing.
tools.example: Review a landing page’s copy and identify ways to improve its signup flow.
tools.distinction: Reusable marketing instructions for compatible agents, including Claude Code and Codex. The agent applies them to your product context.

tools.name: Vercel Domains
tools.purpose: Find, buy and manage domain names. This is where I buy all my domains.
tools.example: Register a domain for a new project and connect it to the deployed app.
tools.distinction: Registration gives you the domain name. Hosting runs the app, while DNS points the name to its destination.

tools.name: Vercel Chat SDK
tools.purpose: Build bots that receive and respond to messages across chat platforms through a shared TypeScript API.
tools.example: Use shared bot logic for an assistant in Slack and Discord.
tools.distinction: Connects a bot to messaging platforms. AI SDK handles model interactions; AI Elements provides React interface components.

tools.name: Vercel AI Elements
tools.purpose: Build AI interfaces with customizable React components for conversations, prompts and model output.
tools.example: Render streaming responses and tool calls in an AI SDK chatbot.
tools.distinction: Provides interface components built on shadcn/ui. AI SDK handles AI behavior and state; Chat SDK connects bots to external chat platforms.

tools.name: 21st.dev
tools.purpose: Discover React components, templates and themes to adapt for your own interface.
tools.example: Find a hero section or pricing layout and bring its component code into a project.
tools.distinction: A community collection of interface designs and code, rather than a framework that runs your app.

tools.name: tweakcn
tools.purpose: Visually customize themes for shadcn/ui interfaces.
tools.example: Try a new color palette and export the theme into your app.
tools.distinction: Changes the styling of your components; shadcn/ui supplies the components themselves.

tools.name: Burp Suite
tools.purpose: Inspect, modify and replay web traffic to investigate security weaknesses in applications and APIs.
tools.example: Test whether your app correctly rejects a request for another user’s private record.
tools.distinction: Tests security behavior through HTTP traffic. Playwright checks browser flows; Burp helps investigate how the app handles unexpected or manipulated requests. Automated scanning depends on the Burp edition.

tools.name: Awesome
tools.purpose: Find topic-specific collections of tools, libraries and learning resources through an index of curated lists.
tools.example: Explore lists for self-hosting, React or developer tools when researching a new project.
tools.distinction: A directory of curated lists. Follow a topic to discover individual projects and resources.

scenarios.name: A paid web app
scenarios.description: One possible selection: build the interface, add sign-in, save records, take payments, send email, test user journeys and deploy. This is an example selection, not a complete production architecture.

scenarios.name: An AI conversation app
scenarios.description: A possible combination for a conversational experience, with optional voice and an avatar. The underlying AI model/provider is an additional choice; voice and avatar services are not required for text chat.

scenarios.name: My everyday workspace
scenarios.description: The environment around the work: coding agents, a runtime, desktop tools, email and hardware. This is an ecosystem across setups, not a claim that every tool runs on the same operating system.
